name: crypto_selftest
description: Prove the installed encryption readers on synthetic samples and record exactly which pairs worked: the receipt an image's acceptance step reads. A program on PATH or a module that imports is not a reader that works. The tool builds the smallest LUKS1, LUKS2 (with its SHA-256 header checksum), BitLocker-metadata (a boot sector with three metadata block offsets), Core Storage, APFS-container (with its Fletcher-64 object checksum), ZIP-with-a-WinZip-AES-extra-field and fixed-VHD samples from the formats' descriptions under its output directory (a rerun in the same job never replaces a sample: the same bytes keep their name, any other bytes take the next free one), runs the real readers on the sample each should read (`cryptsetup luksDump` and `--dump-json-metadata`, `bdeinfo`, `fvdeinfo`, `fsapfsinfo`, `7z l -slt`), and says per pair `parsed` (the reader exited 0 and printed the marker that sample must give), `not parsed` (with the exit code or the missing marker), `unavailable` (the program is not on PATH, named) or `timed out`. Each pair carries the program's version, argv (the sample shown as <sample>) and exit code. It imports `pybde`, `pyvhdi`, `pyluksde`, `pytsk3`, `dfvfs` and `pyAesCrypt` in a child interpreter (isolated mode, so nothing is imported from the working directory), with the module version and an open test on a sample (for pyAesCrypt, a file encrypted and decrypted again with a key made for the run, the module checking the HMAC); a module that is not installed is `importable: false` and its open test `not run`. It lists john and the `*2john` helpers on PATH by name, with john's banner and whether it is a jumbo build: an inventory only, nothing is run but john itself, and whether a skill uses the helpers is not decided here. A VERDICT IS ABOUT THE SYNTHETIC SAMPLE ONLY: a reader that does not parse a sample may be at fault, or the sample may be (the samples are the smallest headers the descriptions allow, and a real reader can ask for more); a parse says nothing about a real volume. `complete` means every sample was built and every reader and module was run to a verdict (including `unavailable`); `partial` means a step timed out or the tool's clock ran out. The first `limit` records are inline and every record is in the JSON Lines file the answer names. No evidence is read, nothing is extracted, no key is used (the AES Crypt key is random, made for the run, passed to the child on its stdin and never printed). Its own clock (`max_seconds`, 90 by default, at most 100) is below the manifest's timeout and each reader or module test is given at most 15 seconds and ended with what it started; it stops on SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP with one JSON answer and exit 128 + the signal, ending the program it started first. Withholding is by shape, measured on random draws per shape planted in a member name or path (rates, not guarantees). Printed whole in 0 of 1,000 draws: hexadecimal ids of 16, 32 and 64, numbers of 10 digits or more, recovery passwords written with dashes, spaces, dots, underscores, no separator or one to three of any other characters between the groups (an en dash, a comma, a colon, a pipe, a tab), also when the groups are cut at the separators of the path (123456-123456/123456-...), full-width, split by invisible characters, or with one decimal digit glued to the first or last group, AWS access key ids, password= and api_key: assignments, user-info, 4x4 groups of capitals and digits joined by - or ., letters and digits of 8, 9, 12, 16 or 40 characters that hold a capital, a small letter and a digit, and a full-width id. Printed whole in some draws: uniform draws of letters and digits (every character as likely a capital, a small letter or a digit as any other) of 8 characters about 2.5%, of 9 about 2%, of 12 about 1%, of 16 about 0.6%, of 24 at most 0.1% and of 40 none; random lowercase letters and digits of 8 about 7%, of 12 about 2.4%, of 16 about 0.4%; 24 random letters 1.5% to 2.6%; a 16-character base32 id 2.2% to 3.4% (by alphabet); four groups of four lowercase hexadecimal digits joined by underscores 4% to 9% (by how the draws are made); an id of 12 or 16 characters whose letters are half Cyrillic or Greek look-alikes about 1%. NOT recognised, by design, and printed whole: an identifier of 7 characters or fewer, a number of 9 digits or fewer, a lowercase-only run of up to 22 letters (it reads as a word), an all-capital letters-only run of any length, three groups of four or five capitals and digits joined by - or . (a rule for them would also withhold upper-case constants such as OpenSSL manual page names), a recovery password cut by anything other than a separator or with a letter in it or glued to it (the groups then show), a ten-digit number written 3-3-4, an e-mail-like lowercase string, and a secret of any other shape; a file whose secrets matter is read in a job run with secret_output: true. What the rule is given is bounded: a string of more than 4096 characters (as written or after folding), a path of more than 8192, or a string with a / and a run of more than 256 name characters is withheld whole as '<text too long to judge withheld>' and not judged (the slowest string inside the bound that a search found took 0.13 CPU s). The output check, which reads every printed string once more, is narrower than the rule: with the rule removed it replaces recovery passwords (full-width ones too), AWS ids, password= values, PEM headers, user-info, hexadecimal of 16 digits or more and runs of 24 or more characters that flip between letters and digits, and it lets through numbers of 10 to 20 digits, ids of up to 23 characters, some base64 (about one in five of 32 bytes), every recovery password whose groups are joined by anything but a hyphen, underscore, dot, space or nothing, and every recovery password cut over the components of a path (the first layer alone holds those). The rule also changes names that are not secrets: of the file names of a documents tree 6.9% have a part withheld (10-digit timestamps, UUIDs) and 0.6% of its directories, of an application tree 16% and 3.1% (a word with a digit inside, such as libmp3lame, is withheld in part). A name, a path, a URL or a message that quotes a credential is withheld with the identifier-shaped strings, from version 2: a value given to a password, token, secret or cookie name (password=..., Pwd=..., a Cookie header), a Name/Value pair in text whose Name is a credential (a number, an array or a long Value too, and the NewValue after an OldValue), a -Password style switch, the argument of ConvertTo-SecureString, curl -u user:pass, mysql -uUSER -pSECRET, a bcrypt hash and the known token families; the text is replaced by a marker that holds only its length. Before, only identifier-shaped strings (tokens, key ids, user-info) were withheld, so these were printed. Known gaps: a pair whose Value is an array nested in another or longer than 4,096 characters, a crypt hash that is not bcrypt, and a secret that has neither a credential name nor a token shape. Each reader's output is read from a file this tool redirects it to: a process a reader (or a version probe) leaves behind is ended before it is read; every answer that is not a refusal or an error carries `program_group` (subreaper, left_behind, unproven, notes), and a `complete` answer is `partial` when a process was ended and when the host cannot rule one out (not Linux, or the kernel refuses PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER).

limit.description: Records returned inline (default 100, 1 to 1000); every record is in the file all_results names

max_seconds.description: The tool's own time limit in seconds (default 90, 1 to 100; the manifest's timeout is 120)
